statement_analysis.reason: The oversight breakdown was structural as well as administrative — the hereditary Iqta reform under Firuz Shah created entrenched Iqtadars who had both the incentive and the political leverage to resist central auditing, regardless of any individual Wazir's competence.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin Khilji's jama-hasil auditing system was the most rigorous central oversight mechanism applied to Iqtadars during the entire Delhi Sultanate period.
statement_analysis.reason: Alauddin's system — combining the Mustakhraj, periodic inspections, and mandatory surplus remittance — represents the high point of central control over Iqtadar revenues in Sultanate history.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Statement 2 has a structural-incompetence false dichotomy may hesitate, and those who know Statement 1 reversed jama-hasil may feel confident marking only (a), selecting (b) prematurely.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Jama and hasil are reversed — jama = assessed demand, hasil = actual collection. This is NOT correct.
Statement 2: 'Entirely a product of administrative incompetence, unrelated to structural features' — this absolute framing is wrong; structural causes (hereditary Iqta) were primary. NOT correct.
Statement 3: Alauddin's system as the most rigorous oversight in Sultanate history — this is historically well-supported. Correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct → answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the single most common jama-hasil confusion. Students who encounter this pairing frequently may have memorized one version without certainty — the reversal (jama = actual, hasil = assessed) is the trap that Statement 1 plants. Statement 2's 'entirely unrelated to structural features' qualifier is a scope-extension trap that turns a partially correct claim (incompetent officials also contributed) into a false absolute statement.
solution.final_explanation:
The jama-hasil distinction is an anchor factual point in Sultanate fiscal history that UPSC has exploited multiple times.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Jama = assessed/demand revenue (what the state required); Hasil = actual revenue collected (what was actually remitted). The statement reverses these definitions — a common and dangerous error.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: The oversight breakdown was not merely administrative incompetence. The structural entrenchment of hereditary Iqtadars under Firuz Shah gave them both incentive and political leverage to resist audits. The statement's absolute clause ('unrelated to structural features') renders it false.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Alauddin's combination of the Mustakhraj, dagh-chehra verification, Diwan-i-Wizarat audits, and mandatory surplus remittance constitutes the most comprehensive oversight framework of the Sultanate period.

Value Addition:
• Memorize: J for Jama = 'Judged' (assessed demand) / H for Hasil = 'Harvested' (actual collection) — a mnemonic for the most confused pairing.
• The gap between jama and hasil was the key metric — a large gap indicated either under-collection or over-declaration of difficulties by Iqtadars.
• Under Firuz Shah, this gap widened systematically as auditing capacity declined alongside hereditary entrenchment.

solution.concept_anchor: Trade-off efficiency vs. revenue control in Iqta fiscal model
solution.strong_distractor: a — A student who recalls Alauddin's strict auditing may select (a), reasoning that the state can recover direct revenue control through oversight mechanisms — missing that the question asks about the inherent structural vulnerability.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The scenario describes a structural vulnerability, not one fixed by adding auditors — Alauddin's auditing was a partial solution, not a cure for the fundamental agency problem.
Eliminate (b): Expanding the number of Iqta assignments worsens the oversight problem by increasing the number of principals to monitor, not solving it.

Confirm (c): The structural vulnerability in delegating revenue collection is the classic principal-agent problem — the delegate (Iqtadar) has incentives to retain more revenue than permitted. Without effective monitoring, delegation means loss of state revenue control.
Eliminate (d): Converting Iqtas to Waqf would shift the problem rather than resolve it — Waqf revenues were also outside direct state control.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario describes a pure principal-agent dilemma inherent to all delegated revenue collection systems, including the Iqta.

The structural vulnerability: when the state assigns revenue collection rights to a delegate (Iqtadar), it gains administrative efficiency but loses direct control over what is collected. The delegate has both information asymmetry (the state cannot perfectly observe collections) and incentive misalignment (the Iqtadar benefits from retaining more and remitting less).

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Deploying more auditors addresses symptoms but cannot eliminate the structural incentive misalignment — Alauddin's auditing reduced but did not eliminate the problem.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Expanding Iqta assignments increases the number of agents to monitor, worsening the oversight challenge.
• Option (c) — Correct: The inherent structural vulnerability is the principal-agent problem — the delegating authority (Sultan) cannot perfectly monitor the delegate (Iqtadar), who has incentives to under-report collections and retain surplus. This is why the system was 'inherently unstable' regardless of who administered it.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Converting Iqtas to Waqf merely changes the category of revenue loss — it does not address the structural monitoring problem.

Value Addition:
• The principal-agent framework is increasingly used in UPSC Mains answers on administrative history — knowing it analytically strengthens answers.
• Alauddin's partial solution (auditing + Mustakhraj) reduced but could not eliminate the agency problem — an important qualification.
• The same structural vulnerability recurs in Mughal Jagirdari: Jagirdars under-reported collections just as Iqtadars had.

solution.concept_anchor: Bahmani revolt Timur invasion Sayyid period sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Timur's invasion caused catastrophic decline may place it before the Bahmani Sultanate's founding, not knowing the Bahmani Sultanate was founded in 1347 — over 50 years before Timur's 1398 invasion.
elimination_logic: Bahmani Sultanate founded (1347): This was a direct consequence of Deccan Iqtadar rebellions under Muhammad bin Tughlaq — comes first among these events.
Timur's invasion (1398): Exploited military weakness from degraded Iqta army — comes after the Bahmani founding, under the last Tughlaqs.
Sayyid Dynasty establishment (1414): Installed partly under Timur's influence after the Tughlaq collapse — comes after the invasion.
Correct sequence: Bahmani Sultanate (1347) → Timur's invasion (1398) → Sayyid Dynasty (1414) → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary trap is placing Timur's invasion before the Bahmani Sultanate's founding. Students who associate Iqta-related rebellions primarily with the late Tughlaq period may not realize the Bahmani Sultanate (1347) was founded decades before Timur arrived (1398). This 51-year gap is the key temporal fact that distinguishes prepared from superficially prepared candidates.
solution.final_explanation:
These three events mark the terminal phase of the Tughlaq Sultanate's decline — each linked to Iqta administrative failure at different stages.

Correct sequence: Foundation of Bahmani Sultanate (1347) → Timur's invasion (1398) → Sayyid Dynasty (1414)

• Bahmani Sultanate (1347): Founded by Hassan Gangu following the rebellion of disaffected Deccan Iqtadars under Muhammad bin Tughlaq — the first major territorial consequence of Iqta mismanagement.
• Timur's invasion (1398): Exploited the military vacuum created by Firuz Shah's hereditary Iqta reform, which had degraded the Sultanate's Iqta-based army beyond effective resistance capability.
• Sayyid Dynasty (1414): Installed partly under Timurid influence after the Tughlaq dynasty ceased to control meaningful territory — a direct political consequence of the 1398 catastrophe.

Wrong options (a) and (c) place Timur before 1347, which is historically impossible.

Value Addition:
• The Bahmani Sultanate eventually fragmented into the five Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar) by the early 16th century.
• Timur's sack of Delhi in December 1398 was one of the most devastating events in Delhi's medieval history — contemporary accounts describe the city as virtually depopulated.
• The Sayyid Dynasty (1414–1451) was effectively a rump state — the Sultanate as a pan-subcontinental power had already ended.

solution.concept_anchor: Wilayat Muqti governor-like power fusion of functions

statement_analysis.statement: The expansion of Iqta territories (wilayats) under the Tughlaqs increased the governor-like authority of Muqtis, who came to exercise simultaneous judicial, military, and revenue functions over their assigned regions.
statement_analysis.reason: Tughlaq territorial expansion meant some Muqtis presided over very large wilayats — the combination of judicial, military, and revenue authority in a single office created de facto governorship, a fusion that the Mughal system later attempted to address through institutional separation.

statement_analysis.statement: This fusion of powers in Tughlaq-era Muqtis was identical to the vassal-lord relationship in European feudalism, including the right to sub-infeudation and a formal contractual obligation binding both the Sultan and the Muqti.
statement_analysis.reason: While the functional power of large Muqtis resembled feudal lords, key structural differences remained: no formal vassalage contract, no recognized right to sub-infeudation (Muqtis could not create their own Iqta-holders), and the Sultan could revoke the assignment without legal constraint.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both statements need to read carefully — the strong distractor position is (a) itself, meaning students uncertain about Statement 2's legal precision may still select (a) reasoning that functional power resemblance is close enough.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Tughlaq expansion + wilayat Muqti governor-like authority + fusion of functions — historically supported — Correct.

Statement 2: 'Identical to European feudalism' including sub-infeudation and formal contract — this overstates the similarity; key structural differences exclude Iqta from genuine feudal classification — Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The comparison between Iqta-holder authority and European feudal lords is analytically important but must be qualified carefully.

• Statement 1 — Correct: As Tughlaq territorial expansion created larger wilayats, Muqtis increasingly exercised simultaneous judicial, military, and revenue powers — making them functionally governor-like. The Mughal mansabdari system's partial separation of military rank from revenue assignment was a later attempt to disaggregate this fusion.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The superficial functional resemblance to European feudalism breaks down at the structural level: (i) No formal vassalage contract existed — the Sultan could revoke Iqtas without legal challenge; (ii) Sub-infeudation was theoretically prohibited — Muqtis could not grant portions of their Iqta to create their own subordinate Iqtadars; (iii) The relationship was one of royal discretion, not mutual legal obligation.

Value Addition:
• UPSC Mains frequently asks: 'Was the Delhi Sultanate feudal?' — the answer requires precisely these structural distinctions.
• The key differences from European feudalism: no contract, no sub-infeudation, no heritable rights (until Firuz), no church as a parallel power structure.
• The word 'proto-feudal' is safer than 'feudal' when describing the Iqta system — it acknowledges functional similarities while preserving structural distinctions.

solution.concept_anchor: Alauddin fixed Iqtadar share agrarian protection limits

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin Khilji's attempt to cap the Iqtadar's permissible revenue share was designed simultaneously to protect the peasantry from over-extraction and to maximize the surplus available for remittance to the central treasury.
statement_analysis.reason: Alauddin's revenue-fixing served dual purposes: it placed a ceiling on Iqtadar retention (protecting peasants) while ensuring that anything above that ceiling was remitted to the centre — both objectives were simultaneously served by the same mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: The contractual obligation for Iqtadars to maintain cavalry contingents (hashm) proportional to their assigned revenues created a direct structural link between agricultural productivity and military capacity in the Sultanate.
statement_analysis.reason: Because hashm size was calibrated to revenue, and revenue depended on agricultural productivity, any agrarian distress that reduced collections also degraded the military capacity an Iqtadar could maintain — linking land productivity directly to military output.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin Khilji's revenue-fixing reforms for Iqtadars completely eliminated peasant exploitation by intermediary revenue officials throughout the Sultanate period.
statement_analysis.reason: Alauddin's reforms had significant limitations — Khuts and Muqaddams continued to exercise their own revenue rights, and enforcement across the entire Sultanate was imperfect. The reforms reduced but did not eliminate exploitation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know Alauddin was effective at revenue reform may accept Statement 3 as broadly accurate, selecting (d) without noting the absolute 'completely eliminated' qualifier.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Dual purpose of Alauddin's revenue cap — peasant protection + maximized remittance — is historically grounded — Correct.
Statement 2: Hashm-revenue-productivity linkage is a structural insight about Iqta military-agrarian connection — Correct.
Statement 3: 'Completely eliminated' is a scope-extension that makes this false — Khuts and Muqaddams remained, enforcement was imperfect — Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3's 'completely eliminated' qualifier is the planted scope-extension trap. Alauddin's reforms were genuinely significant for peasant protection relative to prior and later periods — this makes the general direction of Statement 3 feel correct. The absolute qualifier is what renders it false, and only a student reading with precision will catch it.
solution.final_explanation:
The agrarian-military nexus in the Iqta system is one of the system's most analytically rich dimensions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Alauddin's revenue cap was elegantly dual-purpose — ceiling for Iqtadar retention protected peasants from over-extraction, and mandatory remittance of everything above that ceiling maximized central treasury income. The same mechanism served both objectives.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Since hashm (cavalry contingent) was proportional to Iqta revenue, and revenue was a function of agricultural productivity, the system created a direct structural chain: land productivity → revenue → military capacity. Agrarian distress thus had direct military consequences.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: 'Completely eliminated' is the critical qualifier that makes this false. Alauddin reduced exploitation through revenue caps but could not eliminate the parallel extraction exercised by Khuts and Muqaddams, nor could he enforce his rules perfectly across the entire Sultanate.

Value Addition:
• Alauddin's agrarian reforms are among the most discussed in UPSC — but always note they reduced rather than eliminated exploitation.
• The hashm-productivity link means the Iqta system functioned as an integrated agrarian-military economy — not separate spheres.
• Tughlaq-era failures in enforcing hashm obligations can be partly traced to underlying agrarian distress reducing Iqtadar revenues.

solution.concept_anchor: Firuz Shah hereditary Iqta precedent for Mughal Jagirdari crisis
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Firuz Shah is associated with welfare measures and construction may assume his hereditary reform also had stabilizing effects, not connecting it to the precedent it set for Mughal-era Jagirdari crisis.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Firuz's reform did not consolidate central control — it weakened it by creating an entrenched hereditary nobility.
Eliminate (b): The reform destabilized central authority in the long run — it created an entrenched nobility resistant to the centre.
Eliminate (c): While it did accelerate feudalization, that was an administrative consequence — the longer historical significance was its precedent for the Mughal Jagirdari problem.

Confirm (d): Firuz's hereditary Iqta reform set the structural precedent that the Mughal Jagirdari system eventually inherited — the pattern of revenue assignments becoming effectively hereditary (despite formal rules against it) contributed directly to Mughal Jagirdari crisis under Aurangzeb.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the principal trap — students who associate Firuz Shah with large-scale construction and a generally stable reign may assume his administrative reforms consolidated rather than weakened authority. The hereditary Iqta reform's long-term destabilizing effect (entrenched nobility, degraded military, weakened centre) requires precise knowledge to identify, especially when placed against the backdrop of Firuz's apparent administrative achievements.
solution.final_explanation:
Firuz Shah's hereditary Iqta reform is a pivot point in the administrative history of the subcontinent — its significance extends well beyond the Tughlaq Sultanate.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The hereditary reform did not consolidate central authority — it created precisely the entrenched nobility that resisted central directives, precipitating post-Firuz fragmentation.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Administrative stability during Firuz's own reign did not negate the long-term destabilization the reform caused — by creating hereditary nobles, it planted the seeds of future centrifugalism.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: While feudalization of the Sultanate is a consequence, framing it as the primary historical significance undervalues the broader cross-dynastic administrative legacy.
• Option (d) — Correct: Firuz's precedent — that revenue assignments could become hereditary entitlements resistant to revocation — was structurally reproduced in the Mughal Jagirdari system. Under Aurangzeb, the 'jagir crisis' (demand exceeding supply of productive jagirs, nobles resisting reassignment) mirrors the Tughlaq Iqta problem almost exactly.

Value Addition:
• The Mughal jagir crisis under Aurangzeb: too many nobles, too few productive jagirs — a direct structural echo of the Tughlaq Iqta problem.
• Firuz's reform is therefore a connecting thread between Sultanate and Mughal administrative history — a rare cross-dynastic link.
• For UPSC Mains: argue Firuz Shah's hereditary reform as the 'first feudalization' of the subcontinent's revenue system.

solution.concept_anchor: Firuz Shah Waqf expansion revenue loss Iqta dependence
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Firuz Shah's significant expansion of Waqf grants removed substantial agricultural revenue from the taxable pool, contributing to the central treasury's reduced direct revenue capacity.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. Firuz abolished the extra-legal cesses (abwab) and reduced coercive revenue extraction — this is a documented aspect of his welfare administration.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. R (abolition of abwab) and A (Waqf expansion reducing taxable revenue) are two independent policies with independent revenue effects. The abolition of abwab does not explain why Firuz expanded Waqf grants — the Waqf expansion was driven by religious patronage motives, not by the abwab abolition. These are parallel revenue-reducing policies, not a causal chain.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a classic 'both correct but no causal link' assertion-reason trap. Students who correctly identify both A and R as factually true may assume causation exists because both involve Firuz Shah's fiscal policies and both reduce state revenue. However, R describes one fiscal policy (abolition of abwab) that does not explain A (expansion of Waqf) — they are independent decisions with independent motivations. The reversed-causation aspect is that students may construct a spurious narrative: 'abolition of abwab led to compensating through Waqf expansion,' which is not historically supported.
solution.final_explanation:
Firuz Shah's fiscal record involved multiple simultaneous revenue-reducing decisions, but they did not causally flow from one another.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Firuz Shah's large-scale Waqf grants — endowing mosques, shrines, and religious institutions with agricultural revenue rights — effectively removed those territories from the state's taxable pool. This reduced direct state revenue meaningfully.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Firuz abolished abwab (extra-legal levies) and reduced coercive revenue demands as part of his welfare programme — a separate documented fiscal concession.
• Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The Waqf expansion was motivated by Firuz's religious patronage impulses and political calculations regarding the ulama — not by the abolition of abwab. Both are independent revenue-reducing decisions. Option (b) applies.

Value Addition:
• Firuz Shah's revenue-reducing policies created the 'fiscal paradox': reduced direct revenue + relaxed Iqta accountability = central treasury dependent on unreliable Iqtadar remittances.
• The ulama's political influence under Firuz Shah — reinforced by Waqf patronage — is a recurring UPSC theme on Sultanate religion-state relations.
• Waqf revenue exemption is also relevant to questions on Firuz's relationship with the religious establishment and his dependence on their political support.

statement_analysis.statement: During the Slave Dynasty period, the Iqta system functioned primarily as a political instrument to manage and balance the power of the Turkish nobility (Turkan-i-Chahalgani) rather than as a purely revenue-maximization tool.
statement_analysis.reason: Iltutmish used Iqta assignments strategically to reward, bind, and balance the forty Turkish nobles (Chalisa) — it was as much a political management instrument as a fiscal one during this period.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin Khilji's Iqta policy represented the maximum centralization in the system's history — revenue-oriented, anti-noble, with strict auditing replacing political accommodation as the governing principle.
statement_analysis.reason: Alauddin's approach was the antithesis of the Slave Dynasty's political balancing act — he subordinated Iqtadars to fiscal discipline, reduced their autonomy to near zero, and treated the Iqta as a revenue instrument rather than a political concession.

statement_analysis.statement: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's moderate middle path restored the Slave Dynasty's political accommodation model, including allowing Iqtadars to maintain the same Iqta for life without transfer.
statement_analysis.reason: While Ghiyasuddin restored moderate autonomy, he did not revert to the Slave Dynasty's specific political accommodation model — he introduced the incremental demand principle and did not grant lifetime tenure or suspend the principle of transfer (tabdili).

statement_analysis.statement: Under Firuz Shah Tughlaq, the Iqta system came full circle by acquiring hereditary characteristics that represented a more advanced form of feudal tendency than had existed under the Slave Dynasty.
statement_analysis.reason: Firuz's hereditary Iqta reform created entrenched nobility with inherited revenue rights — going beyond even the Slave Dynasty's political accommodation to create a more structurally embedded feudal arrangement, as there was now a legal basis for hereditary claims.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify Statements 1, 2, and 4 as correct may also accept Statement 3 on the reasoning that Ghiyasuddin 'moderated back toward' Slave Dynasty practices, not noticing the specific false claim about lifetime tenure.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Slave Dynasty Iqta as political management of Turkish nobility — historically accurate — Correct.
Statement 2: Alauddin's maximum centralization and revenue orientation — well-established — Correct.
Statement 3: Ghiyasuddin did NOT restore lifetime tenure or the Slave Dynasty model specifically — he created his own moderate middle path — Incorrect.
Statement 4: Firuz's hereditary reform as 'full circle' with more advanced feudal tendency than Slave Dynasty — analytically sound — Correct.
Three statements correct (1, 2, 4) → answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3's trap is the entity-swap between Ghiyasuddin's approach and the Slave Dynasty's specific practices. Students who know Ghiyasuddin 'moderated back' may assume this means he reverted to Slave Dynasty methods, including lifetime tenure. In fact, Ghiyasuddin's moderation was his own distinct policy — lifetime tenure and suspension of transfer were not its features.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of the Iqta through all phases can be read as a grand arc from political tool to fiscal instrument to hereditary entitlement.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Iltutmish's Iqta was primarily a political balancing mechanism — the forty Turkish nobles needed to be managed, and Iqta assignments were the currency of that management.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Alauddin stripped the political function — Iqta became purely a revenue instrument with maximum central oversight and near-zero Iqtadar autonomy.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Ghiyasuddin created a pragmatic corrective path — not a revival of Slave Dynasty political accommodation. He retained the principle of periodic transfer (tabdili) and did not grant lifetime tenure.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Firuz's reform took the arc to its logical conclusion — hereditary rights created a more deeply embedded feudal structure than the Slave Dynasty's politically contingent arrangements, which remained revocable.

Value Addition:
• The arc: political tool (Slave) → fiscal instrument (Khilji) → pragmatic correction (early Tughlaq) → hereditary entitlement (late Tughlaq) is a powerful analytical framework for Mains.
• Tabdili (periodic transfer) was the single most important anti-entrenchment mechanism — its effective suspension under Firuz enabled hereditary consolidation.
• The Turkan-i-Chahalgani (Forty) under Iltutmish were eliminated as a political force by Balban — an early precedent for using Iqta management against over-powerful nobles.

solution.concept_anchor: Firuz Shah Iqta NOT abolished — transformed hereditary

statement_analysis.statement: Firuz Shah Tughlaq abolished the Iqta system and replaced it with direct state revenue collection from all agricultural territories.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the most explicitly flagged trap: Firuz did NOT abolish the Iqta system — he transformed it by introducing hereditary succession. Direct state revenue collection was not his replacement mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: Firuz Shah's policy allowed the sons of deceased Iqtadars, and in some cases their widows through designated proxies, to succeed to the Iqta — marking the formal institutionalization of hereditary succession in the system.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately describes Firuz's hereditary reform — succession was extended to sons and, through slave/son-in-law proxies, to widows. This was the formal institutionalization that changed the system's fundamental character.

statement_analysis.statement: The hereditary Iqta reform under Firuz Shah had no long-term administrative consequence because subsequent Sultans (Sayyid and Lodi dynasties) successfully reversed the hereditary provisions and restored strict service-based assignments.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sayyid and Lodi dynasties did not successfully reverse the hereditary provisions — indeed, Iqtadars under these dynasties enjoyed even greater de facto autonomy, and the entrenched nobility pattern persisted, contributing to the regional fragmentation that ultimately enabled the Mughal conquest.

solution.strong_distractor: b — The question asks for NOT correct statements; students who identify Statement 1 as incorrect may stop there and select (a), forgetting to check Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Firuz Shah did NOT abolish the Iqta — this statement is NOT correct.
Statement 2: The succession mechanism (sons + widow-proxy) correctly describes Firuz's reform — this statement IS correct.
Statement 3: The claim that Sayyid/Lodi Sultans successfully reversed hereditary Iqta is historically false — NOT correct.

Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct → answer is (b) ... wait: options must match. Statements 1 and 3 are not correct → we need the option that says '1 and 3 only'. Check options: the correct answer designating Statements 1 and 3 as NOT correct is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the most prominent UPSC trap in this entire topic: the claim that Firuz Shah abolished the Iqta system. This is explicitly false — he transformed it. Statement 3's trap is more subtle: students who know Firuz's hereditary reform was historically significant may assume later dynasties corrected it, not knowing that the Sayyid and Lodi periods saw even greater Iqtadar autonomy. The combination of these two incorrect statements amid one correct statement tests whether students identify both incorrectness and the precise historical trajectory.
solution.final_explanation:
Two of the three statements contain significant factual errors that UPSC frequently exploits.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Firuz Shah did not abolish the Iqta system — this is the single most important factual point in this topic. He preserved the system while fundamentally changing its character from service-based to hereditary. No wholesale shift to direct state revenue collection occurred.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The hereditary succession mechanism — sons inheriting directly, widows continuing through slave or son-in-law proxies — is accurately described and represents the operational mechanism of Firuz's reform.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The Sayyid and Lodi dynasties not only failed to reverse hereditary Iqta provisions — they presided over even greater Iqtadar autonomy and de facto territorial fragmentation. The pattern set by Firuz accelerated into the 15th century, creating the conditions for Babur's relatively easy conquest in 1526.

Value Addition:
• Babur's Baburnama notes the fragmented character of the Lodi Sultanate — local chieftains with near-autonomous territories were partly a legacy of Firuz's Iqta transformation.
• The Lodi Sultanate itself ended partly because of the inability to compel loyalty from entrenched Afghan nobles — a structural echo of the Firuz-era Iqtadar entrenchment.
• 'Transformation not abolition' is the single most important phrase to remember about Firuz Shah and the Iqta system.
